headline: Wamphassuc boulders at first light: bass hugging the rocks, first bonito scouts push into the Sound
subhead: Peanut bunker are pouring through the boulder fields from Ram Island to Watch Hill, and the first bonito of the year showed right where we said they would.
body_markdown:
The bait tells you everything if you slow down enough to watch it. This week off Wamphassuc Point I sat the skiff dead still on the pole for twenty minutes before I made a cast, just watching peanut bunker stack up in the current seam behind a boulder the size of a Buick. They were nervous, balling tight, then scattering, then balling again — the way bait moves when something bigger is working the rocks underneath them but hasn't committed yet. That's the tell. When bunker pin themselves against structure like that in Fishers Island Sound in August, there's a bass sitting in the shadow of that rock waiting for the tide to push the bait into its mouth instead of chasing it down.

Water's held a real gradient across the Sound this stretch — New London reading around 70, noticeably cooler than the western basin — and that cooler eastern water is exactly why the rock game has stayed a dawn-and-dusk proposition rather than an all-day bite. I've been on the water by 5:15, poling the skiff over the boulder fields between Ram Island and the Wamphassuc side before the sun gets hard on the water. Bass are there, but they're tucked tight to structure, not roaming open sand. Soft plastics — 5-inch white or bone Slug-Go rigged weightless, and 4-inch chartreuse-back paddle tails on 1/4-ounce jigheads — worked slow and bumped off the rock faces have out-produced anything with more hardware. You want the lure ticking the top of the boulder, not swimming three feet over it. Fish to 28 inches have come off that pattern, most on the last hour of the outgoing before dead slack, when the current stops shoving the bait around and the bass can finally pin it.

The breakwater at Stonington has fished the same way — a slack-tide, structure-hugging bite rather than a blitz. I had two guys out Wednesday morning working bucktails tipped with Gulp along the inside face of the breakwater on the last of the ebb, and we scratched out a handful of bass in that 24-30 inch window along with two shorts we put back. Nothing to write home about in terms of numbers, but quality fish holding tight to rock, which is the honest read on this water right now — not a blitz, a grind, and you need to fish the rocks correctly to get bit.

Now the news that matters: bonito scouts showed in Fishers Island Sound this week, right in the corridor we flagged as imminent a few days back — the Race, this Sound, and the Vineyard rips were the sequence, and here they are, first fish confirmed exactly where we said they'd show. Watch Hill Reef is the classic early address for this, and I had a report of a small pod working bait on the surface off the reef on a calm morning mid-week. Nobody's sticking numbers yet — these are scouts, not a run — but if you want to be the guy who connects first, get a fly rod or a light spinning outfit rigged with a Deadly Dick or a 1-inch Albie Snax on 20-pound fluoro leader and start checking Watch Hill Reef and the eastern edge of the Sound toward Fishers Island on calm mornings. The water's in the right window for it, mid-to-high 70s inshore, and once these scouts feel comfortable they tend to build fast through the back half of August.

Fluke have been the more dependable player this week, and the full moon tide swing sharpened that bite noticeably. The stronger current through the passages and channel edges around Fishers Island Sound is exactly what doormat fluke want — they sit on the edge of the drop where the current sweeps bait past them, and this week's bigger tidal push concentrated them better than the slack water we had two weeks ago. Drifting the channel edges near Fishers Island with 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, has been putting keepers in the box, with a few pushing 4 pounds. Best drifts have come on the last two hours of the incoming, when the current's still got some shape to it but isn't ripping so hard you can't hold bottom.

Black sea bass are steady on the deeper structure off Fishers Island and around the rockier stretches near the reef — small strips of squid or clam on a double-hook bottom rig, standard stuff, but they're there in decent numbers if you want a mixed bag day.

Looking ahead, I'd keep working the boulder fields at first light while this cooler eastern water keeps bass in a tight structure pattern — Wamphassuc, Esker Point, and the inside of the breakwater are where I'm putting my mornings. And I'd start checking Watch Hill Reef on calm days for those bonito scouts to build into something you can actually target with confidence. If the water keeps trending the way it has, the back half of August should turn this into a real run. Doesn't mean it happens on schedule — but that's where I'd be looking, rod in hand, watching the bait instead of the forecast.
